diveTitle: What actually happens when you convert to Word
diveSubtitle: The details that matter once you go beyond the basics.
dive1Desc: Simple documents — paragraphs, headings, basic tables — convert almost perfectly. Complex layouts with overlapping text boxes, unusual font substitutions, or heavy custom design elements sometimes shift slightly, since Word's layout engine and a PDF's fixed layout work differently.
dive2Desc: A scanned PDF is just an image of a page, with no underlying text to extract — converting it directly gives you an empty or image-only document. Our converter automatically runs OCR on scanned pages first, so the resulting Word file has real, editable text instead of a picture.
dive3Title: What you can and can't easily edit afterward
dive3Desc: Paragraph text, headings, and simple tables become fully editable Word content. Complex graphics, charts embedded as images, and precise pixel-level positioning from design-heavy PDFs often convert as images rather than editable objects — they display correctly but need to be replaced to change.
dive4Desc: Multi-column text, like a newsletter or academic paper, converts into Word's own column formatting where possible, preserving the visual layout. Interactive PDF form fields convert to their visual appearance, but the fillable functionality doesn't carry over — you'll see the field outlines as regular elements.
dive5Desc: If the original PDF uses a font that isn't installed on your system, Word substitutes it with the closest available font when you open the file, which can shift line breaks and spacing slightly. Embedding the font in the PDF beforehand, when possible, gives the most accurate substitution.
dive6Title: PDF to Word vs. converting straight to Google Docs
dive6Desc: Converting to Word (.docx) first and then uploading to Google Docs generally preserves more formatting than some direct PDF-import features in other tools, since .docx is a format both Word and Docs read natively. It's an extra step, but usually the more reliable path if Docs is your destination.
faqSubtitle: Everything you need to know about converting PDF to Word
faq1Question: How accurate is the PDF to Word conversion?
faq1Answer: It depends on the type of PDF. For digitally created PDFs — exported from Word, InDesign, or similar — the conversion is highly accurate: text, formatting, and structure all come through cleanly. For scanned PDFs without embedded text, accuracy can vary because an OCR (optical character recognition) step is required.
faq2Question: Will my document's layout be preserved?
faq2Answer: Yes. We work hard to reproduce the original layout as faithfully as possible. Columns, headings, lists, and embedded images are all accounted for. Very complex layouts — like multi-column magazine spreads — may occasionally show minor differences.
faq3Answer: Absolutely. All transfers are encrypted via HTTPS/SSL. Your files are never stored permanently or shared with any third party — they're automatically deleted from our servers after one hour.
faq4Question: How many PDF files can I convert at once?
faq4Answer: On the free plan you convert one PDF at a time, up to 5 MB. Starter unlocks batch conversion — up to 10 files at a time, each up to 20 MB — a huge time-saver when you have a stack of documents to process in one go.
faq5Question: Can I convert the Word file back to PDF afterward?
faq5Answer: Of course. The downloaded .docx file can be opened and edited in Microsoft Word, Google Docs, or LibreOffice, then exported back to PDF or other formats like ODT or TXT. You have complete control over the document.
